utterances.text: Please, did you find out whether anyone went from Cerska to Kravica to help these people; and if they did, how did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were people from Cerska who went to help, because Mr. Semso Salihovic, whom I mentioned before, was visiting the armed groups looking for volunteers to go and help Mr. Golic and the population of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Semso come to Skugrici looking for volunteers?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He spent some time in Skugrici, and he asked for men from our group who wanted to volunteer and go to Kravica with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall Semso's precise words which he said to you when he came to see you in Skugrici? How did he explain the situation?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke at length, and he told us that Mr. Golic and the population of Glogova needed help. He also mentioned that it was in our interests as well in Cerska to help the population of Glogova because we were frequently shelled from the area of Kravica. Also, we found ourselves in a very difficult time when there was literally no food in the area. The only way to extend the agony by a few days or months was to try and obtain weapons and food from the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. From this conversation with Semso Salihovic or with Kadir, who you mentioned, who described the situation in Glogova to you, did you gain the impression that the preparations for going to Kravica, as asked by Semso Salihovic or Kadir, had anything to do with a decision of the subregion or anyone's decision?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We had not succeeded in contacting either the subregion or anyone else in Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did you get any orders to go to Glogova and Kravica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not at that time, and I don't remember having received a written order at any time to perform any kind of task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the fighters of Cerska went there, the armed men of Cerska. Did they go there to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that fact and I know that they did go to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men went there, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I think there were about 50 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there people from Skugrici among them?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this group there were men from Skugrici, I think very few of them, only five or six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, were these men who volunteered to go there or did they receive an order from someone to go there?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to repeat once again, these were men who went there exclusively as volunteers. In that period, nobody could have ordered anyone to go to Kravica and carry out the task in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Semso Salihovic was in question, could he have ordered you in Skugrici to go to Glogova or Kravica? I'm referring to your group, not to individuals.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. Had anyone issued an order I'm sure they wouldn't have obeyed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because throughout this period all activities were voluntary and because the men trusted the leaders who had been with them throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you something about that group in particular, the one that went there. Were you in this group of people who went with Semso to the area of Glogova and Kravica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this group with Mr. Semso Salihovic, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge was Besir Aljukic there?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Besir Aljukic was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the people of Cerska followed this group of armed people or not?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can never forget that. People from all sides went in the direction of Konjevic Polje, or rather Kravica. I think that at that moment no one had stayed at home; everybody set out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, as far as Skugrici is concerned, did you try to stop the people from Skugrici, telling them not to go? Did you consider that to be risky?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. It was highly visible, there was snow. The artillery could target them. We tried to prevent them from going but absolutely did not succeed in this. I'm only sure that they could have been stopped at gunpoint, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were on the 7th of January, 1993? You were describing columns of people. Where did you watch this from, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember very well. On the 7th of January, 1993, I was at Tumace, I mentioned that locality earlier on as well, and from there, there is an excellent view of most of the area of Skugrici, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and the area towards Kravica. I repeat once again that it was snowy. The visibility was very good. So from all sides vast masses were moving about, men, women, children, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except for these columns of civilians, women, children, et cetera, could you see what was going on in Kravica? Did you have binoculars on you or not?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a pair of binoculars from the beginning of the war. My relative who was a hunter gave me these binoculars and that's how I managed to see what was going on. I saw quite clearly how projectiles were being fired from Kravica itself, from Siljkovici and from the surrounding hills. Soon after that there was a great deal of noise throughout the valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Tumace?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, that is to say the 7th of January, 1993, I was at Tumace almost until night fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber why were you at Tumace actually?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there for a single reason with a group of armed men. If there were to be any Serb attacks, we could intervene on time and we could not be caught by surprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you spent the day at Tumace. On that day, the 7th of January, 1993, until night fall, did you see Kravica burning?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see Kravica burning at all. On the surrounding hills I saw one particular plume of smoke or two, but I don't think that it came from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, when these people came back, these people who had left Skugrici as volunteers, that's what you said, did you talk to them about fighting?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they tell you? Where was it that they fought?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that together with a group led by Mr. Semsudin Salihovic they fought at Siljkovici. And from there, they managed to repel the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same Siljkovici you mentioned as the location from where the artillery was constantly firing at Cerska?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the place from where Cerska was being shelled all the time until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you found out from them whether they managed to capture an artillery piece or any weapons?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. Quite a bit of infantry weaponry was seized - I don't know the actual numbers - and also a ZIS was brought in from Siljkovici. This is the gun that we mentioned yesterday, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Serb document?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the document that you showed me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, do you remember what was going on over the following days. Were you at Tumace or not?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the following days - practically the following ten days, I'm almost sure of that - columns of people, thousands of people were streaming towards Kravica trying to get food and trying to continue the agony of their lives, as I mentioned a few moments ago, as there was a total shortage of food where they lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you know that civilians went there over the seven days after the 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that I lived in the area. I saw civilians who brought food in, transported it in different ways. So there was a lot of snow, as I said, but then they managed to drag supplies from Kravica on the snow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether civilians got killed this way?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were many such cases. I remember one particular case. I attended his memorial service. Aljo Korkutovic is the name of the deceased. He went to Kravica and he didn't come back for a day or two. Later on his wife and his relatives found out that a corpse was there. They brought him back from Kravica dismembered. He was at the entrance into a Serb house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out what his actual cause of death was?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that with any degree of certainty, but on the basis of what the body looked like, most probably he tried to enter a house that had been mined because there was visible damage on the house where he got killed, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, this case of house-mining, was it an isolated case or have you heard of other such cases?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not an isolated case. Unfortunately there were many, many more such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from food that you said was brought in from Kravica, did you notice civilians bringing something else in over the next several days?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did notice that a lot of people brought roof tiles because an enormous number of houses had their roofs damaged from the shelling. Also, they brought in doors and windows in particular because there was very, very little glass on any windows. They were all shattered during the shellings of Cerska and Skugrici in the spring and summer. Also people brought in cattle feed and many other things they could find there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As you were describing the situation there, the broken roofs, the lack of doors and windows, you meant the roofs and windows and doors in Cerska. Right?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Skugrici, that is to say in Muslim settlements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, now I'm going to ask you about something different. Did you have any knowledge as to whether anyone had planned an attack on Kravica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no knowledge whatsoever, and I'm not aware of anyone ever planning any kind of activity like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the role of Ferid Hodzic that could be linked to these events in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the role of Muhamed Cikaric in these events?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for Muhamed Cikaric I did not even know him at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the role of Naser Oric in these events?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely did not know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you the following. Did you work as an investigator on a project of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1996 and 1997 that has to do with combat operations of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this question is not clear to me at all. Can you clarify what this means, being an investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you research data on a project of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had to do with the combat operations of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war? During 1996 and 1997, did you work on that project?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never. I never worked on any such project.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness P88. This is a form, a list of combat operations pertaining to Kravica, and it also has an ERN number, 02621529.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last page, the first entry where it says "Ejub Dedic." Could you please have a look at this. It says "Ejub Dedic," and then underneath it says "researcher." Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you look at the handwriting on this entire form. Did you fill it out?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at everything that is written on the left-hand side of the last page of the document. Can you tell whether the handwriting is the same or not? Everything that is written underneath your name, 1, 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth to tell, the handwriting on the left-hand side seems very, very similar to me. I think that this is the handwriting of a single person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you recognise anybody's signature here?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps we could place the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- that's why I was intervening because I think that is appropriate for us to be able to follow better and for the public to be able to follow better.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I asked you whether you recognised any of the signatures of the other signatories.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recognise any of these signatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the date here. Tuzla, the 29th of May, 1997. And it says "the 28th Division" down here. Can you remember May 1997 and who the commander of the 28th Division was at the time?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well. The commander of the 28th Division in the period that you are referring to now was Mr. Salih Malkic, nickname Sale.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please try to raise the document a bit so that the signature can be seen. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, did you have occasion to see Salih Malkic's signature, the commander of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this his signature?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely no, it doesn't even bear a resemblance to his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you whether you know anything about this particular form and similar forms. Is there anything that you can recall in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what it is that you can remember.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that in the mentioned period, in the period that is written in the document, Mr. Aljukic and I were asked to come to the division by a young man. I can't remember his name. I think he worked at the 28th Division. We sat with him and he told us that in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina there was a project underway about some activities and that units -- or rather, about what units and groups did during the course of the war. According to what he said, it was my understanding that he wanted Mr. Aljukic and me to try to help him in that endeavour so that he could do the job. After that, he went on talking about that, and in relation to these documents pertaining to the project, as you mentioned, he referred to Kravica most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that he asked you about particular battles, Kravica included?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He mentioned other ones, but Kravica most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that he was asking about how these combat activities evolved?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had a notebook, and he put some questions to us in terms of what happened and how things happened, where, how many people were there, how many weapons were there, questions of that nature. Since Mr. Aljukic and I pointed out that neither one of us were direct participants in this activity, we said that we could not give him this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I'd like to ask you the following now. Did you tell this gentleman the same things that you told us today in relation to Kravica, that you only viewed certain things going on from a distance?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you tell him exactly?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him the date, I told him where I was, I told him what the tentative number of people involved was, because I didn't know the exact number, when they went, when they came back, what happened after these activities in Kravica. Only what I told you during the course of the proceedings, before I received this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what Mr. Besir Aljukic said, a person you know well, right?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well that he said the same thing that I said to you just now, that he was not a participant there, that he cannot give any information regarding what this gentleman was interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. To the best of your knowledge, did Besir Aljukic work on this project?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely. He worked at an elementary school at the time. He was not in the military at all. He worked in an elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But what I'm asking you is the following: After talking to this particular man from the 28th Division, did you ever talk to Mr. Besir Aljukic about this? Did you ever comment on this project?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After we left this gentleman, we discussed the project and this document, what was -- what this was all about. I didn't quite understand it anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if I have understood what you said. You are talking about a form. Did you see a form that was filled out the way we see it here and now or did you see an empty form?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until now I did not see this kind of filled-out form. There's some numbers here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to the numbers.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I just held an empty form in my hands. It was not filled out, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, you mentioned these numbers now. Can you have a look at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these numbers. For example, look at page 1 where it says the forces of the subregion and then number 150 and the Kamenica detachment number 100, then Bratunac-Milici Brigade, 500. Then please move on to page 3. Look at the engaged forces, 250; and then manpower, about 500 Chetniks; and then light weapons, about 500; heavy weaponry, 20. Could you please tell us something about these numbers. Can you give us your comment. Are the figures always rounded off? Do you have a comment in this regard?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's incredible that all the numbers were rounded off, as you just said. Personally I think that they were written just like that. It's absolutely arbitrary, unfounded. Somebody just wrote it pro forma in order to have this form filled out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, did you hear of 50 Serb combatants being killed in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first I have ever heard of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can take the document from the witness now. Could the usher please somehow the witness another document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. While the document is prepared -- which document do you want to show the witness so that we prepare it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which document is it? Is it a new document or an existing exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] New document, a new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead with your question, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, could you please put back the last page of the Bosnian version. This is signatures. Now, Mr. Dedic, you told us that the names on the left side are written -- seem to be written by the same hand. Do you only refer to the very left side or would you also say that the names right of the left side -- to the left side are of the same hand? Do you know what I mean? You see your name, Ejub Dedic, and then right further on you see it again, and the same is done in all the other cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And would you suppose that all of these names are written by the same hand, the left line as well as the right column of names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, if you allow me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's understood it. I just want to make sure one thing, that what you're saying basically means that whoever wrote down the names on the left-hand side of the left part of this document also, according to you, wrote those signatures afterwards or next to those names? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. It's very similar. I find the handwriting under number 1 and 2 very similar on the right-hand side, whereas the third one is a bit less discernible because it's very small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that I am understanding correctly because your question, Judge Eser, is very important. Look at the first two, all right. There is under [B/C/S spoken] there is number 1, Ejub Dedic. And then next to it there is Dedic. While Ejub Dedic is an indication of the name, "Dedic," which is next to it seems to be the signature of that person. Then there is Mirsad Sulejmanovic, and that indicates who the person is. And then next to it there is Sulejmanovic, a signature of supposedly this Mirsad Sulejmanovic. Are you telling us that you believe that all this, all that appears under number 1 and 2, that is the indication of the name plus the signature, was done by one person and not by two different persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I can see, I think that it is the handwriting of a single person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And are you also as categoric as you have been so far with regard to the next list now -- no, no, no, it's -- sorry, the name side. Besic and -- I can't read it -- Becirevic and Mevludin. There you see -- what is KC and KV? What does that mean? Ms. Vidovic, if you can help us, what does KC and KV mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that KC could mean commander of a company and KV could be [B/C/S spoken], platoon commander, as far as I understand this. However, Your Honour, I think there may be a misunderstanding. I asked the witness whether he signed it and I asked him about the names that were written; I did not deal with it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did make a statement that to him the handwriting on both sides was identical or similar, and we need to clear this because if what is -- he is saying is correct it is a forging of signatures and you can't classify it in any other different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's not an expert at the same time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's telling us that according to hip --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I trust Your Honours aren't trying to take a point of credibility against this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not all; I'm just establishing what he wants to tell us. I'm just establishing what he wants to tell us. Because telling us that it's the same signature on the right and on the left to us is not exactly clear, and that's why I thought the question by Judge Eser was very pertinent and important. And now he's confirming that, according to him at least, as regards 1 and 2, whoever wrote it -- according to him -- I'm not taking it as an expert opinion or -- or an affirmation of -- that this is so. He is not -- and I don't think he's come here pretending to be a calligraphic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm trying to follow the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The relevance being that he is telling us that these documents are not to be taken as genuine documents signed by the persons who are allegedly to have signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But only an expert can say whether a signature is a forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He said what he said about the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're not moving further than this. It's just to establish what he meant when he said that the handwriting on both sides was similar. Right. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify what you saw. Is it in your handwriting and is the signature yours? Let's clarify that. When it said "Dedic, Ejub," was that your handwriting and was the signature your signature?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the first and last name Ejub Dedic and the signature that follows it, this is certainly not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're quite sure that it's not the signature of the commander of the 28th Division down here?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dedic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the witness now -- could the witness be shown a document issued by the command [Real time transcript read in error "commander"] of the Drina Corps. It's a combat order the number is 0284986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The commander or the lieutenant colonel? Because the commander, I think, was someone else - no? - of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am saying the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I got it as the commander, at least if you look at line 10 it says "witness be shown a document issued by the commander of the Drina Corps." That's why I pointed that out. I accept it that you mean the command. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this document bears the number 04284986 and the title is "combat order" issued by the Drina Corps chief of artillery to the commander of the KAG. And I will quote point 1. "In counter-offensive operations the enemy has managed to take part of the territory that had previously been controlled by corps units and has inflicted serious losses on our units, the sector of Sase, Kravica, Mount Glogova, Skelani, Sehitovi [phoen], the general Rudo sector." Mr. Dedic, you were familiar with the situation in the Cerska area and you had information about what was happening in Glogova, which you received from the person you mentioned, and you spoke to the men fighting in the Kravica area. So my question is as follows: To the best of your knowledge, according to what you saw and heard, is it correct what it says here that the enemy - and this refers to the Muslims - has managed in counter-offensive operations to take part of the territory that had been controlled by corps units including the area of Kravica and Glogova. According to your experience was this a Muslim counter-offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The content of this document in this respect is correct; that is, what is mentioned in this order in this connection is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now out paragraph 2 of the same document. "The task of our Corps is to use auxiliary forces on the current lines to tie-up the enemy forces as much as possible, and to use main forces to switch to active combat operations on the following axes: Milici - Suceska - Podravanje village, Zvornik - Kamenica - Cerska, Olovo - Kamenica village, Rudo - Medjedja village, and Rogatica - Medjedja village. Be in a state of readiness defence immediately and for attack by 0600 hours on the 24th of January, 1993." Please, do you remember January 1993 in the Cerska area were you attacked on the 24th or thereabouts in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember well. We were attacked throughout January 1993 but towards the end of this month the attacks grew much more intense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally I will read paragraph 3 of this documents which says: "The KAG composed" -- and you told us that KAG -- well, can you tell us again what KAG refers to, if you know.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The acronym means corps artillery group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The KAG group, composed of the 133-millimetre Howitzer battery bVBR, 122-millimetre shob, 152-millimetre th, shall support the active operations of the Corps' main forces on the following axes: Milici - Suceska village - Podravanje village, and Zvornik - Kamenica - Cerska as required, and shall use barrage fire if requested to prevent surprise breaches by strong enemy forces at the main points of effort in the defence." In these attacks in January 1993, did Serb infantry attacks get support from artillery, as mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes in this respect what the document states is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may this document be given a Defence Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document, Ms. Vidovic, will be given Defence Exhibit number D825. It consists of two pages in the Serbo-Croat and two pages in English. The ERN number is 04284986 to 987.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember what happened from end of January 1993 onwards in the areas of Cerska and Konjevic Polje, briefly?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation from the end of January onwards deteriorated very fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This entire area of Cerska, Pobudje, Konjevic Polje, did it come under attack?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The entire area was attacked on a daily basis, and the encirclement grew ever tighter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in mid-February 1993 or around that time, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Around the middle of February the situation in Skugrici and Cerska areas became so bad that it was really a cause of concern because there was constant shelling -- there were constant infantry attacks. The population began to flee towards Konjevic Polje. They couldn't get through. They came back. And unfortunately, many of them were killed or seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell Their Honours when the Serbs finally managed to break down the resistance of Cerska?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The resistance of Cerska was finally completely broken down at the end of February and in the first ten days of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the people?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the takeover of this area by the Serb forces, the people set out toward Konjevic Polje -- excuse me. May I go on? Before the arrival of these unfortunate people, they were already deluged with refugees and had problems similar to ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any events at the crossroads on the way to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The crossroads at Konjevic Polje, which links Zvornik, Vlasenica, and Srebrenica, was a place where dozens of people were killed or wounded. I saw corpses and carcasses along the road. A lot of personal effects scattered about, parts of human bodies. According to what I saw, there must have been at least 50 dead in one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dead?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened to the elderly and infirm who on that day did not manage to flee from Cerska, including the old men who remained in the Cerska primary school?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the situation had rapidly deteriorated I went to Cerska where my brother was. He was working in the Cerska doctor surgery, and we barely managed to reach the school which was some 200 to 300 metres away from the health centre. And we couldn't get in because there was shelling from all sides. As I had been in Cerska before, I knew that there were about 20 elderly and infirm people inside the school. They couldn't move. We were unable to help them unfortunately and they remained behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't -- or rather, unfortunately I don't know that any of these people survived. I'm not aware that any of them turned up alive afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war, to this day?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To this day I don't know of any survivors from that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you personally aware of the fact that the events in Cerska, including the murder of the elderly men in the primary school in Cerska, was reported to Philip Morillon? Who arrived at that time.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain of that. I personally saw Mr. Morillon and at that time he went to Cerska in an APC escorted by several uniformed soldiers wearing blue helmets on their heads. He went there at our request, the request of the local people, to see what was happening in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, before we go on, my question to you was, it's not all in the record: Did you know that Philippe Morillon who had arrived there with his collaborators had been informed of this?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew very well that he was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his collaborators, were they told of this?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about what Mr. Philippe Morillon, with his associates, did in this connection?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By your leave I'll repeat briefly what I said. He and his associates went in an APC in the direction of Cerska, and in Cerska he stayed only a few hours, in my estimation. And I was there when he came back from Cerska, and I recall well that he said that the situation on the ground in Cerska was not nearly as bad as the Muslims had described, that it was much better, that there were many houses which could be inhabited, although there were houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you, Muslims, respond to this? What was true in fact, what you are telling us today or what Morillon said then?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Morillon, in my view, didn't see what was going on there or didn't want to see what was going on. The truth is what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please play a video clip. It's part of P427 [Realtime transcript read in error "P426"], 3284122. I wish to mention that we have prepared a transcript which we will distribute and we have also given it to the interpreters so that the interpreters can read it in accordance with Your Honour's ruling of yesterday. We are now waiting for the transcript to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. The Trial Chamber appreciates that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not hearing the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, are you receiving interpretation of what His Honour said?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's make sure that the interpretation is functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for pointing that out. I couldn't have known about it if the witness himself doesn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving -- okay. Mr. Dedic, are you receiving interpretation of what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we can go ahead. Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you play the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will show part of a video clip beginning on 44.12 to 46.52.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think we need to ask the booth for sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not receiving any sound myself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the sound is too low and that we can't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the part of the Prosecution, do you contest the transcript in English that we have here? Because if you don't accept it as reflecting what is being said in Serbo-Croat on the screen, we obviously have to find a remedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please bear me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if it is possible -- what I can suggest is this because I know that the media player that is being used has a limit, and beyond that it doesn't go. But our earphones, they can amplify the reception. So if -- I'm just suggesting for a while that we go through the first part again when allegedly Semso Salihovic is speaking, and everyone tries to augment or to increase the sound level of the earphones that we are using.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would be very important for the witness to have the volume turned up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but usher can help him. In the meantime, please, while this is being done I suggest that no one speaks so that we take care of each other's eardrums.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is what they're going to do with the Chetniks up there. They're going to ask for how many days these people are going to be able to keep up? These people have no where to go ... Is Serbia really stronger than the world, or has the world decided to choke these people? Really if you could make any sense of it, could you tell me? "I'm only one Dusko. I'm not the whole world. "I know you're not." Your Honour, the interpreters note that this is inaudible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it for a moment. I agree. I mean, I have got my volume full on and I can't hear a word in -- that is being said on the screen. Yeah, but the important thing is that the witness needs to hear the words that both this gentleman over here and allegedly Semso Salihovic are saying. I mean, I could follow part of Semso Salihovic's speech, but I couldn't go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if there is. I mean, I'm not a technical man. I mean, I can use my ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in fact it's what Semso Salihovic is saying that matters to us, but I think we heard this well in Bosnian. I did. Let's hear what the witness says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard what Mr. Salihovic was saying very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you want to proceed and -- yes -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, the interpreters will bear with us. Again, I suggest that we try to increase the volume to the maximum and that no one speaks after we have done that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Does the world know that these people are choking? ... The world knows what to do to choke Islam in this region. The world sends Philippe Morillon, who is a true Chetnik ... And what the people here are fighting with, 30.000 people? They are fighting with small guns. Do you know how many fighters I lost for this gun? Exactly ten fighters."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's sufficient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please, did you manage to hear what Semso Salihovic was saying?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, is this Semso Salihovic, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, this is Mr. Semso Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, from this part of the video clip from what he himself is saying, did you understand him to be saying that the international community is -- has been tolerating the actions of the Serbs for a year and that they have been given permission to destroy the Muslims in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. area? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I heard and understood that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His standpoint, his attitude of mistrust towards Morillon and his associates, does it reflect the attitude of the people in the areas of Cerska and Konjevic Polje toward Morillon and his associates, at least to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge -- the answer is absolutely yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dedic, is it quite clear from what Semso Salihovic said to the representatives of the international community that the Muslims in the area were being faced with extinction?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this extinction actually occur?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, it did occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what you who were in the area during 1992 and 1993 saw and experienced, was it completely clear to all of you that you were threatened with destruction?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm completely sure of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Semso Salihovic said here -- he said something else as well. He showed a rifle and he said: "Can you see ten people were killed for this rifle?" Tell Their Honours to what extent this is correct, what Mr. Salihovic was saying, that people paid for weapons with their lives?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm with certainty that ten men were killed for the rifle that Mr. Salihovic was showing. He probably knows that. But I am quite certain that not a single rifle we captured or took from Serb soldiers in various ways fell into our hands without being paid for by at least one human life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men in your estimation after the events we saw on this video clip and after the Konjevic Polje and Cerska, how many people went to Srebrenica in early March 1993?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact number because no one knew the precise number of these people. But I am sure that there were several tens of thousands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours briefly what happened in March and April 1993 in the entire area.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The arrival of vast numbers of refugees from Zvornik, Vlasenica, and Bratunac municipality in Srebrenica was followed by continued Serb attacks on the Srebrenica area. Very soon after that, the Serb forces succeeded in taking control of most of Srebrenica municipality so that thousands of additional people who had been living in their villages in Srebrenica municipality now came to the centre of the town of Srebrenica. In these attacks, the Serb forces were so close to the town of Srebrenica on one side that they could target people with a submachine-gun in front of the department store which is in the centre of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what could you say about March 1993, what word would you use to describe it, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: March of 1993 in Srebrenica meant the total encirclement and blockade of Srebrenica. It was completely, hermetically cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these events, according to your knowledge, was the Srebrenica area demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After this there following the demilitarisation of the Srebrenica area; I know that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for you who had weapons, what did demilitarisation mean?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me personally and for other people who had weapons, demilitarisation meant that we had to hand over our rifle and sleep peacefully because the war was at an end. There would be no more military activity in the area. That's what I understood it to mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hand over your weapons?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were there people who did not hand over their weapons and what happened to these people? Can you describe the actions of the international forces and especially of DutchBat in relation to these people?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know very well that a large number of men who had weapons handed over their weapons right away, but there were also those who didn't want to do that for various reasons. However, I noticed and observed personally that members of DutchBat very often -- very soon began forcibly confiscating weapons from individuals who had weapons. Let me mention one example by your leave, something I saw personally. When Dutch soldiers caught a young man who was carrying a rifle, they pulled him about to such an extent that all the buttons came off his jacket. They confiscated his rifle and then they beat him with fists and with the rifle on his face, and I saw this with my own eyes. And there were other cases like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you personally learn for the first time about the attempts of a military organisation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- I learned about such an attempt in early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what did you find this out, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. People were saying that an order had arrived in Srebrenica from Tuzla that units were to be established comprised of men who had arrived in Srebrenica from various sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of this formation?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember well. In the documents that arrived from Tuzla, this formation was supposed to be called the 8th Operations Group of Srebrenica, and it was supposed to comprise light brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the 1st of January, 1994, did you know of any military activities in Srebrenica, you personally?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew about the activities of the members of the international forces. They were there, they were moving about, doing things, but those were the only activities I observed or knew about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on to my next question, can this transcript be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Madam Vidovic. But before we do that I must register something with regard to the transcript. It seems that -- I don't know which line it is, now I have lost track of it. But the video that we -- an extract of which we followed came on the transcript as -- shown in the transcript as being Exhibit 426, P426. In actual fact it is P427. So for the record that is a correction that I am making myself. This would be now 427.1 --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Registrar, how would you prefer this to be marked, the transcript of --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's a Defence exhibit, so D826.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D826. So this transcript in both languages, in Serbo-Croat and in English consisting of two pages in toto is being marked as Defence Exhibit D826.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, did Ferid Hodzic come with you from Cerska to Srebrenica, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well. Mr. Hodzic, when Cerska fell into Serb hands, did not go towards Srebrenica. With a rather large group of men, I think that there were about 200 of them based on what we've known since then, went in the direction of Kladanj and actually arrived there with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mirsad Sulejmanovic, in this case named Skejo, the leader of the group from Skugrici go with you?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Mirsad Sulejmanovic, Skejo, when this group fell took an even larger group of people, most of them young, armed, went to Tuzla via Baljkovica. So he was not there either and he didn't try to enter Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened to the group from Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do remember. Also, a large group people from Kamenica did not come to Srebrenica. They went to Tuzla. I'm sorry, let me just finish. Among the groups that were leaving this area that were not going to Srebrenica, there were people from Konjevic Polje, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just clarify the matter. When we are talking about these groups, is it your understanding that I'm asking you about armed groups. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, armed groups. Because covering a couple of hundred kilometres unarmed would have been totally impossible and unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could P31 please be shown to the witness now. This is a document of the 1st of January, 1994, from the General Staff of Sarajevo. It is called organisational changes, formation of RJ, in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please, look at this document. It is dated the 1st of January, 1994. "I hereby order: "Organisational Changes: "Formed the 8th Operations Group in Srebrenica," and then the light brigades that you mentioned. And finally I will stop at subparagraph F. "Establish the 284th Eastern Bosnian Light Brigade with its headquarters in Srebrenica, according to T-412.240. The newly formed brigade will have numerical code and T-31329 and VJ number 6342, its mobilisation duration will be 20 hours. A unit in charge of the mobilisation plan will be 284th Light Istocnobosanska Brigade. The 284th Light Eastern Bosnian Brigade will consist of the 114th Eastern Bosnian Brigade, the 1st Cer Detachment and the 6th Detachment of Kamenica." Please, as you were giving evidence a few moments ago, you said that a large number of people precisely from these groups out of which the 284th Light Brigade was supposed to be established went to Tuzla and Kladanj, including the commanders, the persons you called leaders of groups, rather. Ferid Hodzic, Sulejmanovic, Skejo. Please, as you read this document, can you reach a conclusion as to whether people in Tuzla and Sarajevo had the right kind of information at all about the situation in Srebrenica on the 1st of January, 1994, when this was written, when this order was written.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Because most people who took part in the war who were young, who were able-bodied, who had weapons, left. It is primarily people who did not dare venture on such a journey came to Srebrenica. So they came for completely different reasons. So there were very few people in Srebrenica at all who had participated in the war in Cerska before its fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, what about the 114th Eastern Bosnian Brigade, what did that denote, if you know?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was the name for armed groups from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, while giving evidence several times you said that you had occasion to travel to Konjevic Polje. During the course of 1992 until the fall of Konjevic Polje in March 1993, to your knowledge was there a brigade there from a military point of view, in the military sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never. I wish it did exist, though. What was there had nothing to do with what a brigade would really look like from a military point of view. There would have to be military facilities, barracks, trained personnel. A brigade has to have professionals, proper personnel. They'd have to have logistics, too, and they didn't have any because Cerska -- it was under a total blockade. So there was no appropriate personnel and there weren't any logistical possibilities for establishing a brigade. It could have only existed in name, but there really was nothing that could be called a brigade there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, during January in 1994, were you called somewhere to talk about the establishment of the 284th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was called by Mr. Veiz Sabic. I remember he was there. Then I remember there was a man from Kamenica. Trso was his name. His leg was shorter. I don't remember his first name. We sat there and talked about the establishment of brigades in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, do you know whether any of you had received orders in writing in terms of an appointment to any post in this brigade?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for myself, I can say for sure that I never received any order appointing me to any post in this brigade. As far as I know, I'm not aware of anyone else having received such orders either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember what Veiz told you about what you were supposed to be in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. He said to me that in that brigade I should be appointed Chief of Staff of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, did you take any measures? Did you do anything that can be related to the establishment of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did work. We started making lists of these persons, able-bodied men, who arrived from these areas to Srebrenica. We wanted to see who it was that arrived, what age they were, et cetera. In my opinion, this was a list of men who were in the territory of Srebrenica and that's what it was basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, when you wrote these lists of these men who would belong, say, to the 284th Brigade, did you have in mind any previous participation in fighting or did you simply make lists of people who were present there right then?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We simply recorded people who arrived in Srebrenica, who happened to be there after these persecutions, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "people," are you referring to able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, able-bodied men who had come to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, to the best of your knowledge, what about the other so-called brigades that you saw on paper here, was the same done basically? Were such lists made?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked amongst ourselves because we were in a relatively small area. The situation was the same, identical, in other cases, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, can you describe to the Trial Chamber how in this situation of demilitarisation this brigade functioned until the fall of Srebrenica, with the exception of what you said just now that you listed the persons or personnel involved.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again very clearly, there were no military activities as far as this brigade is concerned or any other brigade. Everything that was done in this domain was to list able-bodied men, and I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, everything that was done was -- was it on paper or --

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that was done in relation to the brigade that is mentioned here was only on paper. There was absolutely nothing in practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me ask you now, as regards this brigade, the 284th Brigade, did you ever get your own barracks, logistics?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I wish to point out once again that in Srebrenica there are no barracks. The only logistics we had in Srebrenica at all was Operation Parachute. Most of us made torches out of paper and cellophane and went out at night, and those were the greatest activities that we were engaged in, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, do you remember whether you report reports to anyone about the activities of the brigade higher up, say to this 8th Group?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any point. Why should we write reports when we did nothing? I don't remember writing any report except that perhaps sometimes we may have said to someone, We have the list that was required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, did you have a military police and a security organ established as such? I am referring to the 284th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no military police then because the existence of the military police and its functioning was explicitly forbidden once the international forces arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Security organ?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was one man, one person, who was appointed security organ on this list that I mentioned, Fadil Dedic, a man who worked in the bauxite company. On paper he was there, but he didn't do anything in this regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, in 1993 and 1994, what did you do yourself? Did you do anything else except for what you told us now about Operation Parachute?

utterances.speaker: EJUB DEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, when possible, I also worked at the elementary school because I am a teacher by profession. So that was what I mainly did, working at school and providing food for myself and for my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the witness to look at a document now, unless it's too late. I don't know what your plan is. How long should we work today? Well, then P280 can be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I were to voice the wish of everyone present, I would probably ask you to stop here. But however, I think we can afterward to dedicate a couple of more minutes to finish with this next document and then you can wind up for the day. All right. How long is it going to take you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would be very happy to break off at this point because I am a bit tired myself and I believe that the witness must be tired, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't blame you, Madam Vidovic. I think everyone is. So we'll give you a rest, Mr. Dedic. How much more time will you require tomorrow, more or less? I'm asking you in order to give Mr. Wubben an indication.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to half an hour, not more than half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Given that Ms. Vidovic is -- sticks to that schedule, do you think you would be in a position to finalise your cross-examination by the end of business on Friday, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you so that if you're not we'll make arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to give you a guarantee like such, but it seems to me what whenever it is 30 minutes that I might -- might finalise, and I'll do my best for that. But again, no guarantees given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Dedic will now be escorted out of the courtroom. Please, may I remind you of my recommendation to you, or my order to you, not to communicate or let anyone communicate with you with regard to the subject matter that you are testifying about. Thank you. Tomorrow we are sitting in the morning. I think it's in this same courtroom. Yes. 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
